product.pattern: Adjacent market: what's the natural next segment after your current users?
product.source: Crossing the Chasm, Blue Ocean Strategy

product.pattern: Product extension: which feature do power users hack together themselves?
product.source: The Mom Test, Competing Against Luck

product.pattern: Platform play: can your product become the infrastructure others build on?

marketing.pattern: Under-served channel: where do your customers already hang out that competitors ignore?
Story gap: what belief about your category is widely held but wrong?
marketing.source: Building a StoryBrand, Made to Stick

marketing.pattern: Earned attention: what can you do that's so remarkable people talk about it unprompted?
marketing.source: Contagious, Purple Cow, The Tipping Point

sales.pattern: Up-sell path: what do your best customers naturally need next?
Partnership distribution: who already has your customer and isn't competing?

strategy.pattern: Strategic inflection point: is a technology/market shift creating a new game where you have an advantage?
Unbundling opportunity: which part of an incumbent's bundle can you do 10x better?
strategy.source: Business Model Generation, Zero to One

strategy.pattern: Counter-positioning: can you adopt a model the incumbent can't copy without hurting themselves?

vision.failure: No written mission statement — team operates on unstated assumptions
Mission is vague platitudes ('world-class excellence') — nobody can act on it
Mission changes every quarter — no persistent north star
Mission exists but founder never references it in decisions
Can't describe where the company will be in 5 years with specificity
Vision is purely financial ('$100M ARR') — uninspiring, no product/impact story
Vision too small — incremental improvement vs category creation
Vision too grandiose — no bridge from today to the vision
No explicit company values — culture is whatever the loudest person says
Values are aspirational, not behavioral ('integrity' but no one gets fired for violating it)
Values are different from what's actually rewarded
vision.book: What Got You Here Won't Get You There (Goldsmith)

vision.failure: Values not used in hiring, firing, or promotion decisions

strategy.failure: Don't understand the 5 forces shaping industry profitability
Entering an industry with no barriers to entry — margin erosion inevitable
Ignoring substitutes — competing only against direct rivals
Don't know supplier/customer power dynamics in own value chain
No systematic competitor tracking — rely on anecdotes
Competitor analysis is a one-time exercise, not ongoing
Only track direct competitors — miss adjacent/new entrants
TAM inflated by including customers who won't buy
No bottoms-up market sizing — only top-down analyst reports
Addressable market is real but too small to build a venture-scale business
Competing in an existing category without differentiation — price war inevitable
No category creation — being compared to incumbents on their terms

product.failure: Building before validating the problem exists
Solving a vitamin problem, not a painkiller problem
Problem validated with friends/family who won't be honest
Not understanding that 'I would buy that' ≠ an actual purchase
Asking 'would you use this?' instead of 'when did you last try to solve this?'
Interviewing the wrong persona — not the economic buyer or end user
Talking to customers once at the start, never again
Designing for personas, not the job the customer is hiring the product for
Don't know what customers were 'firing' before using your product
Product competes against 'doing nothing' and loses
MVP is too polished — months spent perfecting an unvalidated feature
MVP is too crude — doesn't demonstrate the core value prop

marketing.failure: No ICP — 'anyone who can benefit' which means no one specifically
ICP defined by demographics, not behavior/jobs-to-be-done
ICP changes every quarter because no one sticks with a bet long enough
Same message sent to all segments — nothing resonates
Segments too small to build a real business on
Not segmenting by behavior (usage, spend, intent) — only by firmographics
No mapped buyer journey — content created randomly
Journey is about the company, not the customer's internal struggle
Homepage headline is a tagline, not a value proposition
Message describes what the product IS, not what the customer BECOMES
Jargon and buzzwords — no human would say this out loud
Company is the hero of the story, not the guide

sales.failure: No defined sales stages — pipeline is a list of names with gut-level estimates
Pipeline is inflated with 'good conversations' — no qualification criteria
No pipeline coverage ratio — don't know how much pipeline is needed for target
No qualification framework — chasing every lead regardless of fit
Sales team qualifies on budget only, ignores need/authority/timeline
Sales reps spend 70% of time on deals that never close
Using product-pitch approach for complex B2B sales — needs SPIN/diagnostic
No common methodology — every rep sells differently, no repeatable process
Reps talk features when they should be diagnosing problems
Demos aren't converting — product looks great but no urgency to buy
No competitive battlecard — reps lose deals they should win
Deals lost to 'no decision' — can't create urgency or overcome status quo bias

finance.failure: Don't know runway in months — operating on bank balance, not burn rate
Runway under 6 months with no fundraising plan
Cash flows not forecast — surprised by payroll
Don't know CAC, LTV, or payback period
LTV/CAC ratio under 3:1 — each dollar of sales/marketing loses money
Gross margin below 50% — can't afford sales & marketing at scale
No budget — spending as requests come in
Budget built on hopes, not pipeline coverage or retention rates
Zero-based budgeting never done — inertia keeps dead costs alive
Raising too much or too little — not matching round to milestones
Raising from the wrong type of investor for the stage
Fundraising is a full-time job for 3-6 months — company stalls
finance.book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things (Horowitz)

operations.failure: Critical processes live only in key people's heads — single point of failure
No SOPs — every time a task is done, it's done differently
Processes documented once then never updated — reality has drifted
Founder is the bottleneck — everything needs their approval
No constraint analysis — don't know what's limiting throughput
Hiring to fix bottlenecks without first fixing the process
Manual data entry across multiple systems — error-prone and slow
Automating a broken process — digitizing chaos doesn't fix it
Single supplier dependency — one failure stops the business
No vendor scorecard — quality issues discovered by customers
Race to the cheapest supplier — quality and reliability sacrificed
Stockouts — losing sales because inventory wasn't reordered

hr.failure: Hiring before defining what success looks like in the role
Job description is a wishlist, not a set of 3-5 outcomes the person must achieve
Hiring a generalist when you need a specialist, or vice versa
Only hiring from your network — limited candidate pool
Passive sourcing only — no active outreach to the best people
Interviews are unstructured conversations — no scorecard, no consistency
Hiring based on likability, not demonstrated ability to deliver the outcomes
No work sample or trial project — hire on interview performance alone
Skipping reference checks — the 'we need them now' trap
References are cherry-picked by the candidate — not back-channeled
No structured onboarding — new hire gets a laptop and a 'figure it out'
New hire productivity delayed by months — cost of poor onboarding invisible

customer_success.failure: Customers take 3+ months to see value — churn before they get there
Onboarding is a feature tour, not guided to the customer's specific outcome
No defined 'aha moment' — don't know when a customer is actually onboarded
No implementation playbook — every deployment is bespoke chaos
Data migration breaks — customer starts with corrupted data, never recovers trust
No early warning signals — churn is a surprise every time
Not tracking health score — don't know which accounts are at risk
Churn is measured; churn reason is not — fixing symptoms, not causes
Renewal conversation starts 30 days before expiry — too late to demonstrate value
Renewal is a sales transaction, not a success milestone
No save playbook — every at-risk account gets ad-hoc treatment
Escalation to exec doesn't close the gap — they can't fix the product

technology.failure: No architecture decisions recorded — why was this choice made?
Monolith that should have been split 6 months ago — velocity collapsed
Premature microservices — added complexity without the scale to justify it
No tech debt tracking — it's invisible until everything breaks
Codebase has no tests — every change is Russian roulette
Refactoring never budgeted — always deprioritized for new features
Manual deployments — releases are stressful all-day events
Deploy frequency under 1/week — can't ship fixes fast
No on-call rotation — founder fixing things at 3am
Incidents are fixed but never post-mortemed — same issues recur
No data warehouse — analytics run on production DB, slowing everything
Data is siloed — marketing can't see product data, sales can't see usage

data.failure: Tracking everything, understanding nothing — dashboard overload
KPIs are lagging indicators (revenue) not leading indicators (pipeline created)
Vanity metrics celebrated (downloads, signups) while business metrics ignored (activation, retention)
Every team tracks different definitions of the same metric — 'active user' means 5 things
No single source of truth — 3 dashboards, 3 different revenue numbers
Decisions made on gut feel — data exists but not consulted
Decisions made on a single data point, not a trend — month-over-month noise mistaken for signal
Analysis paralysis — more data requested instead of making the call
No A/B testing — every change is 'we think this is better'
A/B tests run but never reach statistical significance before shipping
Board deck takes 2 weeks to produce — data isn't readily available
Monthly reports are backward-looking only — no forward indicators

brand.failure: Brand = logo + colors. Nobody on the team can articulate what the brand STANDS FOR.
Brand identity changes with every redesign — no consistent equity built
Marketing promises are bigger than what the product delivers — trust destroyed on first use
Brand promise not defined — customers have no expectation, so no reason to choose you
No recognizable logos on the website — prospects think the product is unproven
Case studies hidden behind forms — can't build trust anonymously
Founder has no public presence — brand IS the founder in early stage
Content is generic — no original point of view, nothing to build trust around
No crisis plan — when something breaks, response is reactive and damaging
Data breach / outage communicated late — customers find out on Twitter first

partnerships.failure: Partnerships are random — whoever shows up, not whoever creates the most leverage
Partnering with companies that have misaligned incentives — they win when you lose
Partner gives 10% and takes 80% of the economics — bad deal hidden in bad math
Revenue share doesn't cover the cost of serving the partner's customers
Resellers signed but never sell — no enablement, no incentive to push your product
Channel conflict — direct sales team competes with partners
Integration is shallow — doesn't provide enough value for either customer base

growth.failure: No defined growth model — don't know whether growth is viral, paid, content, or sales-driven
Growth is linear when it should be compounding — no flywheel designed
No viral/referral loop — every customer acquired through paid channels
Paid acquisition scales but retention doesn't — growing a leaking bucket
Entering new country as if it's the same as home market — localization ignored
Expanding to too many countries at once — spread thin, win nowhere
Moving upmarket without the product/process maturity to serve enterprise
Moving downmarket cannibalizes the core business
Product can't be tried without talking to sales — PLG impossible
Free tier cannibalizes paid — conversion rate too low to sustain
Signups are high, activation is 5% — product doesn't deliver the 'aha' fast enough

leadership.failure: Founder burnout — working 80-hour weeks with no end in sight
leadership.book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things (Horowitz)

leadership.failure: Founder is the bottleneck — every decision routes through them
No advisor/peer group — founder has nobody to be honest with
leadership.book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things (Horowitz)

leadership.failure: Founder avoids the hardest conversation — letting go of a co-founder or key exec
leadership.book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things (Horowitz)

leadership.failure: Decision paralysis — waiting for perfect information that will never arrive
Reversible decisions treated as irreversible — massive time wasted
Decisions not written down — same debates happen every week
Founder doing $15/hour work while $150/hour decisions go unmade
Calendar driven by others — founder has no maker time
Working IN the business, not ON the business
Micromanaging — founder reviews every code commit / email / slide
Abdicating, not delegating — 'you figure it out' without context/support
